extracted.intended_audience: general news readers interested in business / legal / consumer-safety stories
extracted.subtask_description: A news report summarizing an individual plaintiff's lawsuit against McDonald's for burns from spilled hot coffee, placing the case in historical context by comparing it to the 1994 Liebeck v. McDonald's litigation and noting legal and factual factors that bear on liability and damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligence for improperly secured lid
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff alleges workers were negligent for improperly securing the coffee cup lid, causing the spill and resulting burns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negligence here is framed as failure to follow safe handling procedures; evidence may include eyewitness testimony, store procedures, and whether employees followed protocols. The article cites the claim in Childress's suit that the lid wasn't put on correctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incident reporting by employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether employees filled out an incident report after the spill (the article notes none of the three employees she spoke with filled out an incident report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of an incident report may be used to show failures in store procedure or lack of proper response to a safety event; conversely, documented reports and immediate assistance may be presented by the defense to rebut negligence claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior incidents / pattern of harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that other customers have been burned (article references testimony that 700 other McDonald's customers had been burned in the Liebeck case).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior incidents can establish notice/foreseeability and support punitive damages; the article uses the Liebeck record as precedent showing pattern and company knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coffee temperature as a factor in liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperature at which McDonald's served coffee (testimony in Liebeck case said coffee was kept between 180 and 190 degrees) and whether that temperature is hotter than industry norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unusually high serving temperatures can increase severity of burns and support claims that the product was unreasonably dangerous; expert testimony on industry norms and burn thresholds is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity and degree of burns / medical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of injury (e.g., third-degree burns in Liebeck; Childress did not suffer third-degree burns or require lengthy hospital treatment) and resulting scarring and pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity of injury and treatment needs are central to calculating compensatory damages and may affect publicity and jury sympathy; the article contrasts the two plaintiffs' injuries to show differences in likely damages/outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensatory damages for medical bills and emotional distress
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff seeks reimbursement for medical bills and claims ongoing pain and emotional distress as a result of the incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensatory damages are intended to cover actual losses (medical expenses, pain and suffering); attorneys often initially seek medical reimbursement and may quantify additional non-economic harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punitive damages and basis for calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury in Liebeck case suggested punitive damages based on defendant's revenue (the punitive sum was tied to revenue from two days of coffee sales; later reduced by the judge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punitive damages punish and deter conduct; juries may consider corporate revenue or prior conduct when setting punitive awards, but judges can reduce them; presentation of corporate conduct and prior notice is key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative fault / plaintiff responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards may be reduced when plaintiff is found partially responsible (Liebeck's compensatory award was reduced because she was found partially responsible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative/negligence rules can diminish recoverable damages; evidence of plaintiff conduct (e.g., how cup was handled) is evaluated against defendant's conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's safety protocols and employee training
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense assertion that restaurants have strict food safety protocols and train crew to ensure lids on hot beverages are secure (statement by franchise owner/operator Peter Ou).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentation of policies, training records, and consistent enforcement can be used to rebut negligence claims; absence or poor enforcement may support plaintiff's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement as common resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases may end in settlement rather than final jury award (article notes Liebeck and McDonald's ultimately reached an undisclosed settlement after verdict adjustments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlements can follow jury verdicts or avoid trial; they may be confidential and can reflect pragmatic resolution rather than legal admission of liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent and attorneys' reliance on prior cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorneys consider prior precedent such as Liebeck when evaluating and litigating current suits ('Anytime an attorney looks at a case, they'll look at precedence that has been set').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior high-profile cases shape litigation strategy, expectations about damages, and public perception; factual differences between cases remain important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public perception and impact on tort reform debate
rubrics_metrics.description: High-profile cases like Liebeck can be widely misunderstood and used by critics to argue for tort reform (caps on damages), while media portrayals shape public views of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative framing can affect jury pools, legislative responses, and policy debates; attorneys and advocates may address or counter popular misconceptions during litigation and press coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product/safety category: hot food temperature litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawsuits arising from the temperature of served food (article notes other recent cases, such as a hot Chicken McNugget causing burns to a child), indicating a broader area of liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature-related food injury claims share common issues: foreseeability, safety practices, injury severity, and corporate knowledge; patterns across incidents can strengthen claims.
